Finding.title: Expression evaluation route executes user input with eval
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The scan claim is directly supported by main.py lines 375-379: the route reads request.form['expression'] and calls eval(expression) inside response construction. No counterevidence shows a restricted globals dictionary, parser, allowlist, authentication gate, or sandbox.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: The /evaluate route accepts POST input and the expression variable reaches eval when supplied. This establishes a reachable source-to-sink path from unauthenticated HTTP form data to Python expression evaluation under the observed code.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is treating request-controlled text as Python code rather than parsing a constrained expression language or binding it as inert data.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerability. Runtime payload execution was not performed, so the exact object access available to a submitted expression remains unvalidated.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: No false-positive condition was identified. The vulnerable sink is not dead code and no effective control appears between input and eval.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability. The finding remains distinct from BF-STD-006 because Python eval and Jinja rendering use different interpreters, routes, and reachable object models.

Finding.title: DNS lookup route concatenates form input into an OS command
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The scan claim is supported by the command helper at main.py lines 171-172, which calls os.popen(command).read(), and the /lookup route at lines 356-360, which concatenates request.form['address'] into 'nslookup ' + address.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: A POST to /lookup can set address. The address value is concatenated into a shell command string and passed to os.popen through rp(). No validation, allowlist, quoting, argument-vector execution, or authentication is visible.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is shell command construction from untrusted request input.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerability. Runtime shell metacharacter behavior was not tested, so backend shell specifics remain an execution-environment question.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: No false-positive condition was identified. The sink is reachable from a route-level form parameter and the helper executes a command string.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability. It is related to other execution-boundary findings but is not a duplicate because the sink is os.popen rather than Python eval or Jinja rendering.
uncertainty: Runtime command processor behavior and exact command injection syntax were not validated.
requiredAdditionalEvidence: Safe local runtime validation with non-destructive commands could confirm observable command execution behavior.

Finding.title: Client-controlled cookie is deserialized with pickle
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The finding is supported by main.py lines 328-329, where request.cookies['value'] is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads. Lines 345-346 show the server creates that cookie format with pickle.dumps, but there is no integrity protection for the client-returned value.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: The GET/POST /cookie route checks for a value cookie on non-POST requests. A browser or HTTP client can provide the cookie, so the deserialization path is reachable without authentication.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is use of Python pickle as a client-side serialization format and later trusting the client-supplied bytes as safe to deserialize.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerability. No malicious pickle payload was executed.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: Base64 encoding is reversible and does not contradict the claim. No signing, MAC, safe parser, or server-side session lookup is present on the read path.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability. It is related to BF-STD-008 through the browser-cookie trust boundary, but the root cause and sink are different.
uncertainty: Runtime payload execution and process-level impact were not tested.
requiredAdditionalEvidence: Safe local runtime validation could confirm payload execution characteristics if authorized.

Finding.title: Greeting route renders user input as Jinja template source
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The scan claim is supported by main.py lines 453-468. request.form['name'] is first interpolated into a string and then that string is interpolated into the Jinja template source passed to render_template_string.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: A POST to /sayhi supplies name. The resulting value becomes template source before rendering. No fixed template with bound variables, sandbox, or pre-render escaping control is visible.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is constructing executable template source from request input rather than passing user data as a template variable.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerability. No Jinja payload was executed, so the exact reachable object graph and code-execution capability were not validated.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: No false-positive condition was identified. The route directly reaches render_template_string with user-controlled template text.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability. It is related to BF-STD-003 through server-side interpretation but remains distinct because Jinja template evaluation has different mechanics and preconditions.

Finding.title: JWT verifier accepts None and HS256 algorithms based on untrusted token header
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The finding is supported by ALLOWED_ALGORITHMS including 'None' and 'HS256', unverified-header algorithm dispatch in verify_token, a None branch accepting an empty signature, and /user using the resulting sub claim for admin state.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: The /user route reads the authentication cookie and passes it to verify_token. Because verification dispatch depends on the token's untrusted alg header, an attacker who can set the cookie can target alternate verification branches. /user/jwks exposes the public RSA key material.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is algorithm agility controlled by untrusted token headers, including acceptance of unsigned None tokens and HS256 alongside RSA verification.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerability. A forged token was not submitted, so exact claim constraints and library parsing behavior were not dynamically confirmed.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: Issuer, audience, and time checks exist, but they are applied to claims that can be attacker-controlled in the unsigned-token path; this does not contradict the vulnerability claim.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability. It is related to BF-STD-001 through cookie trust and to BF-STD-005 through cryptographic misuse, but it is not a duplicate.
uncertainty: No forged JWT was submitted to confirm runtime acceptance.
requiredAdditionalEvidence: Safe local runtime validation could confirm whether crafted None or HS256 tokens are accepted as admin.

Finding.title: Category query parameter is concatenated into SQL
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The scan claim is supported by main.py lines 476-484, where the category query parameter is inserted into a WHERE clause using string formatting and then executed through cursor.execute. Line 594 shows raw SQL statement strings are built for non-Oracle backends.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: The /listservices route accepts category through a GET query parameter. The value is interpolated inside single quotes in SQL and reaches cursor.execute. No parameter binding or allowlisted category mapping is visible.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is dynamic SQL construction from untrusted request input rather than parameterized query execution.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerability. Database-specific payload behavior, multi-statement handling, and privilege impact were not dynamically tested.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: The base query targets public_stuff, but the injected value controls SQL syntax within the WHERE clause. This does not negate the injection path.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability. It is related to deployment/back-end authority modeled by T009, but no duplicate finding exists for that deployment dependency.
uncertainty: Exact impact depends on configured database backend, driver behavior, and database account privileges.
requiredAdditionalEvidence: Runtime validation against the selected disposable database backend is needed to establish concrete impact.

Finding.title: XML parser enables DTD loading and network access for user-supplied XML
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The claim is supported by main.py lines 395-400, where request.form['xml'] is parsed with etree.XMLParser(no_network=False, load_dtd=True, huge_tree=True). Those options permit DTD processing and do not disable network access.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: A POST to /xml supplies xml, which is encoded and passed to etree.fromstring with the unsafe parser configuration. Output escaping occurs after parsing and therefore does not control parser-side resource access.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is unsafe XML parser configuration for untrusted XML input.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports the vulnerable configuration. External entity resolution, file access, network access, and resource-exhaustion behavior were not tested.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: HTML escaping of the serialized output does not prevent XXE or parser-side side effects. No false-positive condition was identified in source.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability as an unsafe parser configuration with plausible XXE impact. Concrete exploit impact remains runtime-dependent.

Finding.title: Config endpoint decrypts attacker-controlled ciphertext and returns padding errors
Finding.evidenceToClaimAnalysis: The finding is supported by the AES-CBC decrypt/unpad implementation at main.py lines 140-168 and the /config path at lines 428-433, where an attacker-controlled key parameter is unhexlified, decrypted, and raw exception text is returned.
Finding.implementationAndReachability: The /config route accepts key through a GET query parameter. When key is present, it reaches decrypt(kv, KEY), and padding exceptions from unpad can be reflected to the response.
Finding.rootCauseAnalysis: The root cause is unauthenticated chosen-ciphertext decryption with CBC mode and externally visible error differences before any authentication or integrity check.
Finding.validationAssessment: Static evidence supports an oracle pattern. Iterative ciphertext testing was not performed, so practical recovery or forgery of config keys remains unvalidated.
Finding.falsePositiveReasoning: The normal page links expose only selected config keys, but the route still accepts arbitrary key parameter values. That does not contradict the chosen-ciphertext path.
Finding.technicalConclusion: Evidence supports the vulnerability pattern. It is related to BF-STD-004 by confidentiality impact and BF-STD-008 by cryptographic security objectives, but it is not a duplicate.
uncertainty: Observable oracle reliability and exploit practicality were not dynamically tested.
requiredAdditionalEvidence: Safe local runtime validation could confirm response distinguishability across chosen ciphertexts.
